title: Leader-Based Consistency
explain: With asynchronous followers, a reader can see stale data, but not randomly. It is a handful of precise anomalies, each with a cheap targeted fix. Replication lag is simply how many committed writes a follower has not applied yet.
model:
| Anomaly | What the user sees | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Not read-your-writes | Posts a comment, refreshes, it is gone | Read your own recent writes from the leader, or by position token |
| Non-monotonic reads | The second refresh is older than the first | Pin a user to one follower |
| Not consistent prefix | An answer appears before its question | Keep causally related writes in one partition, or carry causal metadata |

Also keep apart:

- **Durability vs freshness.** Sync replication to one follower guarantees *that* follower has the write; a read from a *different*, async follower can still be stale.
- **Linearizability** (every read sees the latest committed write) needs reads from a leader that has confirmed its leadership; plain follower reads cannot give it.
- **Lag dynamics:** lag grows whenever the arrival rate exceeds the follower's apply rate, and shrinks only when it has spare capacity.

Reads are routed in the [read path](#/sd/f/leader-based-read-path); commit modes are in the [write path](#/sd/f/leader-based-write-path); the weakest end of the spectrum is [eventual consistency](#/sd/f/eventual-consistency).

details.q: A user posts a comment, reloads from a follower, and it is missing; a minute later it appears. Which guarantee broke?
details.a: Read-your-writes. The follower had not applied the write yet. Fix by reading the user's recent writes from the leader or from a follower that has reached the write's log position.

details.q: A user refreshes twice: the first response has a post, the second does not. Which guarantee, and the cheapest fix?
details.a: Monotonic reads. Two different followers had different lag. Pin the user (or session) to one follower, for example by hashing the user id.

details.q: Questions and answers live on different shards; a reader sees the answer before the question. What is the anomaly and a fix?
details.a: Consistent-prefix violation: causally related writes were replicated independently. Put related writes in the same partition, or carry causal metadata so the reader waits for the cause.

details.q: How big does lag get if the leader commits 2,000 writes/s and a follower applies only 1,800/s?
details.a: It falls behind by 200 writes/s: after 10 minutes, 200 × 600 = 120,000 writes. If the write rate then drops to 1,000/s, it catches up at 800/s net, so 120,000 / 800 = 150 s.

details.q: If one follower is synchronous, can a read be stale?
details.a: Yes. Sync only guarantees that particular follower has the write. A read from another, async follower can still be behind, so freshness depends on where you read, not just on how you write.

details.q: Do these session guarantees add up to linearizability?
details.a: No. They are per-user fixes for visible anomalies. Linearizability needs every read to see the latest committed write globally, which requires reading from a leader that has confirmed its leadership (or a quorum read).

prompts.q: Name the three classic follower-lag anomalies and give a one-line fix for each.
points: Read-your-writes: read own writes from leader or by position
Monotonic reads: pin the user to one follower
Consistent prefix: keep causally related writes together or carry causal metadata

prompts.q: Explain replication lag with numbers: when does it grow, and how does it recover?
points: Grows when write rate exceeds apply rate
Recovers at the spare apply capacity
Monitor lag, alert, shed reads from lagging followers

prompts.q: Explain how durability and freshness differ in leader-based replication.
points: Sync follower guarantees a copy exists, not that all reads see it
Reads from other async followers can be stale
Linearizable reads need the confirmed leader
Choose where to read per use case
